newsitem.title: GREECE: Salomon says Greek shares still look cheap.
newsitem.headline: Salomon says Greek shares still look cheap.

text.p: In an apparent U-turn from a late January report which recommended an underweight position in local currency, Salomon Brothers is now bullish on Greek shares saying they still look cheap despite their recent rally.
In a strategy paper released on Friday, analysts Miranda Xafa and Anastasios Adam note that the long-awaited revaluation of the equities market had arrived.

"Following a relatively quiet year in 1996, the Greek market appreciated 26 percent year-to-date. This long-awaited revaluation was justified by greater political stability, lower inflation and a commitment to EU convergence," the strategy paper said.
Greece's equities market came out of the cold and took off in 1997, one of the beneficiaries of a new flow of funds into European emerging markets.
Year-to-date the Athens stock exchange general share index rose 26 percent in dollar terms, outperforming the IFC Global Composite by 14 percent.

"We expect Greece to continue attracting international investors with the expected continued privatisation this year of its national telephone company -- OTE -- and other major industries," the analysts said.
Foreign and domestic investors stayed on the sidelines for most of 1996 but have moved assertively into the market in 1997, pushing the index to record highs.
Helping boost sentiment were low inflation numbers for January -- 6.8 percent year-on-year from 7.3 percent in December 1996, based on the revised CPI index.
This, it said, encouraged greater confidence in the economy and in the government's ability to achieve its targets.
"While 1996 was a slow year for the Greek equities market, the fundamentals for a rerating were put in place. The country's commitment to EU convergence is no longer in question," The analysts said.
Even a relatively small adjustment to asset allocation by domestic investors, as has been seen year-to-date, will push the equities market to new levels.

While the percentage of mutual fund assets invested in equities remains relatively small -- currently 3.0 percent -- it has contracted over the past two years from 15 percent due to meagre performance of the equities market.
"The shift in asset allocation of domestic balances towards equities and new foreign flow of funds which began in January 1997 is expected to continue throughout the year," Salomon said.

T-bill rates declined to 11.2 percent in the fourth quarter of 1996 from 14.2 percent in the fourth quarter of 1995. In addition, Greek companies have seen a dramatic decline in their cost of capital.
"Since the end of capital controls in April 1994 and the introduction of ecu shadowing in 1996, companies have found it possible to borrow in ecu with modest forex risk," it said.
Larger Greek companies can now borrow at LIBOR plus 1.0 percent in various EU currencies and ecu, compared to borrowing rates of nearly 30 percent in 1994 in local currency.
Also, despite a sizeable inflow of international funds since the beginning of 1997, the average market P/E has risen with the forecasted P/E for 1997 now at 10.9.
"Compared with the January average MSCI Emerging Markets Free Index P/E of 17.4 times and an average EAFE P/E of 15.0 times, Greece continues to look cheap," Salomon's strategy paper said.
